questions.question: A research team is training a 3B-parameter transformer that fits comfortably in one H100 GPU's 80 GB of memory, but projected single-GPU training would take 18 months to reach target loss. The dataset is 3 TB and fits on local NVMe storage. Which signal makes distributed training necessary in this scenario?
choices: Dataset exceeding GPU HBM capacity, which automatically forces tensor parallelism regardless of training time
The physical presence of NVLink inside the node, which makes multi-machine scaling mandatory
Unacceptable wall-clock training duration, even though memory capacity and local storage are not binding constraints
Fault tolerance cost, because single-GPU training cannot survive hardware restarts
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Unacceptable wall-clock training duration. Three signals can independently force distribution: memory exhaustion, unacceptable wall-clock duration, and dataset scale exceeding single-machine storage. In this scenario, memory and dataset storage both suffice, but an 18-month training duration makes the calendar itself the binding system constraint. Choice A misreads the criterion: the dataset fits on local storage, and dataset size alone dictates input pipeline design rather than forcing tensor parallelism. Choice B inverts the logic: NVLink enables intra-node tensor parallelism when needed, but hardware presence alone does not mandate scale-out. Choice D is false because single-GPU training can easily checkpoint locally, whereas distributed systems introduce multi-node failure cascades.
questions.learning_objective: Identify which of the three physical triggers for distributed training fires in a scenario where only wall-clock time is the binding constraint

questions.question: A team doubles a data-parallel cluster from 64 to 128 GPUs and observes that total step time drops by only 12 percent even though the compute term per worker falls by a factor of two. Using the distributed step-time equation $T_{\text{step}}(N) = T_{\text{compute}}/N + T_{\text{comm}}(N) + T_{\text{sync}}(N) - T_{\text{overlap}}$, explain the mechanism behind this poor scaling and what measurement would confirm the diagnosis.
questions.answer: Per-worker compute time halves ($T_{\text{compute}}/128 = 0.5 \times T_{\text{compute}}/64$), but communication time $T_{\text{comm}}(N)$ and barrier synchronization overhead $T_{\text{sync}}(N)$ do not shrink; in fact, collective latency and straggler penalties grow with $N$. As a result, the communication-computation ratio $\rho = T_{\text{comm}}(N) / (T_{\text{compute}}/N)$ increases significantly, pushing the cluster into the communication-bound regime where workers spend most of their time waiting for gradient aggregation. A timeline trace (e.g. via PyTorch Profiler or NVTX) showing AllReduce and barrier wait times dominating step time and exceeding the local forward/backward compute duration would confirm this diagnosis.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how the communication-computation ratio creates a scaling ceiling when per-worker compute shrinks faster than communication cost

questions.question: A 30B-parameter model must be partitioned across 4 server racks connected by 100 Gb/s standard Ethernet. The model exceeds any single GPU's memory, but the full model state fits within the aggregate memory of the racks. Which placement strategy respects the network bandwidth constraints?
choices: Tensor parallelism across the 4 racks, because sharding individual matrices reduces per-device memory most aggressively
Data parallelism with a full model replica per rack, because Ethernet bisection bandwidth removes any need for topology-aware placement
Pipeline parallelism with layer groups assigned to each rack, because only stage-boundary activations cross the slow inter-rack links
Expert parallelism within a single MoE layer, because sparse activation patterns automatically eliminate network bottlenecks
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Pipeline parallelism with layer groups assigned to each rack. Pipeline parallelism transmits only boundary activations between consecutive stages (traffic proportional to $B \times S \times d_{\text{model}}$), which is a low-frequency, point-to-point pattern that 100 Gb/s Ethernet can sustain. Tensor parallelism requires per-layer AllReduce collectives on every forward and backward pass, demanding NVLink-class bandwidth (>900 GB/s) to avoid catastrophic compute stalls; running TP over 100 Gb/s Ethernet violates the bandwidth feasibility check. Choice B fails because the 30B model does not fit on a single GPU/rack replica. Choice D fails because MoE routing requires high-bisection All-to-All communication that would saturate the cross-rack Ethernet fabric.
questions.learning_objective: Select a parallelism strategy whose communication pattern matches the bandwidth class of the inter-device fabric

questions.question: In the 3D Parallelism Cube ($N_{\text{total}} = d \times p \times t$), how do the three orthogonal scaling axes interact to allocate cluster accelerators for large models?
choices: The three axes are mutually exclusive; allocating nodes to data parallelism precludes using tensor or pipeline parallelism in the same cluster
Tensor and pipeline parallelism can compose within a single node, but data parallelism can only be used if model parallelism is completely disabled
The accelerator count is the sum of the dimensions ($N_{\text{total}} = d + p + t$), with each parallelism type requiring a dedicated, disjoint pool of nodes

The axes compose multiplicatively ($N_{\text{total}} = d \times p \times t$), allowing systems to simultaneously shard layers (TP), pipeline stages (PP), and replicate the pipeline across data shards (DP)
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Multiplicative composition of orthogonal axes. Data ($d$), pipeline ($p$), and tensor ($t$) parallelism are independent, orthogonal scaling axes whose product determines the total accelerator count ($N_{\text{total}} = d \times p \times t$). Frontier training configurations routinely compose all three (e.g. TP=8 within an NVLink node, PP=16 across nodes via InfiniBand, DP=128 across the cluster) to satisfy memory capacity, per-layer communication latency, and global throughput constraints simultaneously. Choice A treats the strategies as mutually exclusive. Choice B is false because standard 3D parallelism wraps TP/PP pipelines within outer DP replicas. Choice C confuses multiplicative compositional resource scaling with additive partitioning.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how data, pipeline, and tensor parallelism compose multiplicatively in the 3D parallelism cube

questions.question: A 20B-parameter model exceeds single-GPU memory but fits within a single 8-GPU H100 node whose internal NVLink provides over 900 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth. Applying the chapter's decision framework and bandwidth feasibility checks, which placement is the most defensible default?
choices: Use tensor parallelism across the 8 NVLink-connected GPUs, because the fast intra-node fabric can sustain the per-layer AllReduce traffic
Scale out with pure data parallelism across multiple Ethernet-connected nodes, because data parallelism avoids model-partitioning complexity
Defer distribution entirely until the dataset also exceeds single-machine storage, because model memory alone never justifies parallelism
Use data parallelism with one full model replica per GPU, because replicating the model everywhere avoids inter-GPU communication during the forward pass
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Tensor parallelism across the 8 NVLink-connected GPUs. Tensor parallelism is the natural choice when a model exceeds single-GPU memory but fits within a single node connected by NVLink (>900 GB/s), which can absorb the high-frequency per-layer AllReduce operations without stalling compute. Choice B fails because standard data parallelism requires each GPU to hold the entire model, which is impossible here. Choice C is a fallacy because memory exhaustion alone is an independent, non-negotiable trigger for distribution. Choice D is impossible because an individual GPU lacks sufficient HBM capacity to hold the 20B parameter model.
questions.learning_objective: Apply decision-tree logic from model-memory and interconnect-bandwidth constraints to choose intra-node tensor parallelism

questions.question: What structural property most fundamentally distinguishes distributed training from a stateless distributed web service that handles independent HTTP requests across many replicas?
choices: Distributed training always uses strictly more machines than web serving, because neural networks cannot execute on small clusters

Distributed training requires every worker to maintain a consistent view of mutable model parameters, so gradient synchronization becomes a mandatory coordination step rather than an optional optimization
Distributed training is compute-bound while web serving is always latency-bound, preventing the two workloads from sharing hardware
Distributed training cannot tolerate node failures because synchronization protocols physically prevent checkpoint-based recovery
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Mandatory mutable shared state consistency. Stateless web replicas handle independent queries without requiring consensus on shared state. In contrast, distributed training must produce a single, mathematically coherent set of updated weights after every iteration, making collective gradient synchronization and consistency barriers mandatory. Choice A is false because both small training jobs and massive web services exist. Choice C is a false dichotomy; both workloads face memory, compute, and networking bounds. Choice D is incorrect because production distributed training relies heavily on checkpointing to recover from node failures.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the mutable-shared-state requirement as the structural feature that separates distributed training from stateless services

questions.question: Which sequence correctly represents the causal dependencies of a single synchronous data-parallel training iteration?
choices: 1. Compute forward and backward passes on local shard -> 2. Assign disjoint batch shard -> 3. Synchronize gradients via AllReduce -> 4. Update local parameters
1. Synchronize parameters across workers -> 2. Assign disjoint batch shard -> 3. Update local parameters -> 4. Compute forward and backward passes
1. Assign disjoint batch shard -> 2. Update local parameters -> 3. Compute forward and backward passes -> 4. Synchronize gradients via AllReduce
1. Assign disjoint batch shard -> 2. Compute forward and backward passes on local shard -> 3. Synchronize gradients via AllReduce -> 4. Update local parameters
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Assign shard -> Compute forward/backward -> Synchronize gradients -> Update parameters. Shard assignment must happen first so each worker knows its distinct input data; local forward and backward passes compute gradients based on those inputs; gradient synchronization (AllReduce) must occur before the optimizer step so all workers receive identical aggregated gradients; and the parameter update must happen last to maintain identical model replicas. Choice A violates data causality by attempting computation before receiving data. Choice B attempts parameter updates before computing new gradients. Choice C applies parameter updates prior to synchronization, causing immediate weight divergence across replicas.
questions.learning_objective: Sequence the four causal phases of a synchronous distributed training step and justify their ordering

questions.question: The chapter frames distributed strategies as loop transformations borrowed from compiler optimization. Which transformation corresponds to tensor parallelism?
choices: Unrolling the outer batch loop across devices so each worker processes a disjoint data slice
Vectorizing the inner matrix-multiplication operations across devices, so NVLink acts as a cluster-scale vector register file
Pipelining a sequence of model layers across stages, with microbatches flowing through in an overlapped schedule
Replicating the entire computation across machines so that each worker produces an independent, redundant result
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Vectorization (SIMD) of inner matrix-multiplication operations. Tensor parallelism splits the inner matrix multiplication operations within each layer across devices, effectively acting as a cluster-scale SIMD unit where NVLink provides the low-latency communication analogous to a vector register file. Choice A describes data parallelism (parallel-for on the outer batch loop). Choice C describes pipeline parallelism (instruction pipelining across sequential layers). Choice D describes redundant computation rather than parallel matrix partitioning.
questions.learning_objective: Classify each parallelism strategy by the compiler loop transformation it corresponds to at cluster scale

questions.question: A 1,024-GPU BSP training job reports 180 ms average per-worker compute time but observed per-step latency averaging 340 ms with a p99 of 720 ms, and cluster MFU is poor. Explain the likely mechanism and why it grows worse as cluster size increases.
questions.answer: Bulk Synchronous Parallel (BSP) enforces a global barrier at each gradient synchronization step, meaning the iteration time is strictly determined by the slowest worker (the straggler). Even if 1,023 GPUs finish compute in 180 ms, a single worker experiencing thermal throttling, NCCL link congestion, host memory contention, or OS jitter delays the entire cluster to 340 ms (or 720 ms in p99 cases). As the cluster size $N$ increases, the probability of sampling an extreme outlier in each step approaches 1, magnifying barrier wait times and causing cluster-wide Model Flops Utilization (MFU) to collapse.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how BSP barriers amplify rare per-worker delays into cluster-wide inefficiency as worker count grows

questions.question: A distributed training job begins hanging indefinitely during AllReduce, but only on batches that contain variable-length sequences and conditional computation paths (such as MoE routing). Workers report no CUDA errors and are simply waiting. Which failure mode best matches this signature?
choices: Bandwidth underutilization caused by choosing a tree AllReduce algorithm on a large gradient tensor
Pipeline bubbles created by uneven stage depth across workers
Collective deadlock caused by workers disagreeing on which tensors to synchronize, leaving some ranks waiting forever for messages that other ranks never enqueue
Optimizer divergence caused by stale gradients in asynchronous parameter servers
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Collective deadlock from mismatched collective execution. Collective communication primitives (such as NCCL AllReduce) require every participating rank in the communicator to execute matching collective calls in the exact same sequence with identical tensor shapes; when conditional paths or dynamic routing cause a subset of workers to bypass a collective, the participating ranks block permanently waiting for absent peers. Choice A describes low throughput, not an infinite hang. Choice B describes idle pipeline stages rather than a collective barrier hang. Choice D refers to numerical divergence in asynchronous training, which does not cause execution deadlock.
questions.learning_objective: Diagnose a collective-hang failure caused by mismatched synchronization semantics across workers running conditional computation

questions.question: In standard synchronous data parallelism (such as PyTorch DistributedDataParallel without ZeRO or FSDP), which component is replicated across workers and which is partitioned?
choices: The full model (parameters, gradients, optimizer state) is replicated on every worker, while the global minibatch is partitioned into disjoint shards
The model is partitioned into layer shards across workers, while the minibatch is replicated so every worker processes the same examples
Both the model and the minibatch are replicated everywhere, and only the optimizer state is partitioned to save memory
Neither is replicated because all workers share a remote tensor store accessed over the network on each access
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Full model replicated, minibatch partitioned. In standard DDP, each worker maintains a full replica of parameters, gradients, and optimizer states, while the global dataset/minibatch is split into disjoint shards. Gradients are synchronized via AllReduce to ensure identical weight updates. Choice B describes pipeline/model parallelism. Choice C describes ZeRO-1/sharded optimizer states rather than standard DDP. Choice D describes a remote parameter store model.
questions.learning_objective: Identify which state is replicated and which is partitioned in standard synchronous data parallelism

questions.question: A synchronous data-parallel configuration runs 8 GPUs, each processing a local minibatch of 32 examples before executing a single AllReduce and optimizer update. What is the effective global batch size, and what governs the learning rate scaling when expanding from a single GPU?
choices: Effective global batch size is 256; learning rate should be scaled linearly by 8x (with warmup) if operating below the critical batch size
Effective global batch size is 32; learning rate must remain identical to single-GPU training
Effective global batch size is 256; learning rate must be divided by 8 to prevent gradient explosion
Effective global batch size is 4,096; learning rate must follow an exponential scaling schedule
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Global batch size of 256 with linear learning rate scaling. In synchronous data parallelism, the effective global batch size is $B_{\text{global}} = N \times B_{\text{local}} = 8 \times 32 = 256$. Because gradients from all 8 shards are averaged, the optimizer performs an update mathematically equivalent to a single batch of 256 examples. When below the critical batch size, linear learning rate scaling ($\eta_{\text{new}} = 8 \times \eta_{\text{base}}$) alongside learning rate warmup preserves optimization dynamics. Choice B ignores the aggregation across the 8 workers. Choice C inverts the learning rate scaling rule. Choice D miscalculates the global batch size ($8 \times 32 \ne 4096$).
questions.learning_objective: Calculate effective global batch size and apply linear learning rate scaling principles in data-parallel training

questions.question: The chapter's GPT-2 scaling analysis concluded that 8 GPUs on one NVLink-connected node running gradient accumulation can beat naive scale-out to 32 GPUs across a 10 Gb/s commodity network. Explain the quantitative mechanism that drives this counterintuitive result, naming the relevant bandwidths.
questions.answer: Gradient accumulation achieves a large effective batch size locally by accumulating gradients over multiple forward/backward microbatches before synchronizing over NVLink (600–900 GB/s bidirectional bandwidth), where AllReduce takes only a few milliseconds. In contrast, scaling out to 32 GPUs across a 10 Gb/s (1.25 GB/s) commodity Ethernet network forces a ~3 GB gradient tensor across slow inter-node links, requiring several seconds per AllReduce ($T_{\text{comm}} \gg T_{\text{compute}}$). Scaling efficiency collapses to ~30% on the 32-GPU commodity cluster due to communication overhead, whereas the 8-GPU NVLink node achieves >95% efficiency by keeping communication inside the high-speed fabric.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze why gradient accumulation on one fast-fabric node can outperform scale-out across a weak network

questions.question: A 7B-parameter model in mixed precision requires about 112 GB of total training state (parameters, gradients, 16-bit Adam optimizer states, and FP32 master weights) under replicated DDP, exceeding the 80 GB capacity of an H100. Under ZeRO-3 (or FSDP Full Shard) on 64 GPUs, why does per-GPU memory for this state drop to roughly 1.75 GB?
choices: Because gradients are eliminated entirely and parameter updates are delegated to a central CPU host
Because all tensors are compressed to INT4 during training, eliminating floating-point storage
Because optimizer states, gradients, and parameters are each partitioned across the 64 workers, so each GPU stores only 1/64 of the total state
Because activations are offloaded to NVMe storage, removing the parameter memory footprint entirely
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Partitioning of optimizer states, gradients, and model parameters across workers. ZeRO-3 / FSDP shards all three static training state components (16-bit model weights, 16-bit gradients, and FP32 optimizer states/master weights) across the $N=64$ ranks ($112\text{ GB} / 64 \approx 1.75\text{ GB}$ per GPU). Full parameters are reconstructed dynamically per layer via AllGather just before forward/backward passes and freed immediately after. Choice A describes centralized parameter servers. Choice B incorrectly claims INT4 compression is used. Choice D confuses dynamic activation offloading with static model state sharding.
questions.learning_objective: Compute per-GPU memory for sharded training state and explain how ZeRO-3 / FSDP eliminates parameter replication overhead

questions.question: If a model's parameters, gradients, and activations already fit comfortably in single-GPU memory with high compute utilization under standard DDP, what is the expected throughput impact of enabling ZeRO-3 / FSDP Full Sharding?
choices: Throughput will increase significantly because sharding reduces the per-device gradient memory footprint
Throughput will typically decrease because FSDP introduces additional AllGather collectives before forward/backward passes and ReduceScatter collectives on the critical path
Throughput will remain exactly identical because NCCL completely eliminates communication overhead regardless of collective count
Throughput will increase by exactly the ratio of sharded GPUs ($N\times$)
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Throughput decreases due to additional AllGather and ReduceScatter collectives. ZeRO-3/FSDP is a memory-saving technique, not a communication-reducing one: it adds an AllGather before each layer's forward pass, another AllGather before its backward pass, and a ReduceScatter after backward computation. When memory capacity is not a binding constraint, these extra collective operations add latency to the critical execution path and reduce overall throughput compared to standard DDP. Choice A confuses memory reduction with throughput speedup. Choice C ignores physical network latency and bandwidth limits. Choice D confuses memory sharding with linear compute scaling.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the communication throughput trade-offs of FSDP/ZeRO when memory capacity is not the binding constraint

questions.question: Why did modern production systems (such as PyTorch DDP and Horovod) largely replace centralized parameter servers with decentralized AllReduce topologies for dense synchronous training?
choices: Parameter servers are mathematically incapable of executing stochastic gradient descent updates
Parameter servers can only support CPU workers and cannot interface with GPU accelerators
AllReduce eliminates all inter-GPU communication by computing updates locally without exchanging data
Centralized parameter servers concentrate dense gradient traffic at a single network bottleneck, whereas AllReduce distributes communication symmetrically across all workers
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Elimination of centralized network bottleneck via symmetric communication. In a parameter server architecture with $N$ workers, the server's network interface must ingest gradients from and broadcast weights to all $N$ workers, creating an $O(N)$ bandwidth bottleneck that collapses scaling past a few nodes. Ring and tree AllReduce topologies distribute communication symmetrically across all workers, bounding per-GPU transfer volume to $2(N-1)/N \times M_{\text{grad}}$ regardless of cluster width. Choice A is false because parameter servers implement SGD mathematically correctly. Choice B is incorrect because parameter servers have been implemented on GPUs. Choice C is false because AllReduce requires explicit network communication.
questions.learning_objective: Compare centralized and decentralized synchronization topologies in terms of bandwidth bottlenecks for dense gradient traffic

questions.question: The scaling-efficiency equation decomposes step time: $\eta_{\text{scaling}} = 1/(1 + N(T_{\text{comm}}(N) + T_{\text{sync}}(N) - T_{\text{overlap}})/T_{\text{compute}})$. As worker count $N$ grows large, what happens to efficiency in the limit, and why does an optimal collective algorithm not save it?
choices: Efficiency approaches 100 percent because per-worker compute time falls with more workers

Efficiency degrades as the communication-to-compute ratio $(T_{\text{comm}} + T_{\text{sync}} - T_{\text{overlap}})/(T_{\text{compute}}/N)$ grows, eventually making overhead the dominant step-time term
Efficiency remains constant as long as Ring AllReduce is used, because Ring AllReduce is bandwidth-optimal
Efficiency only improves if SGD is replaced with Adam, because Adam reduces gradient communication size
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Scaling efficiency collapses as communication overhead dominates per-worker compute. In the scaling efficiency denominator, per-worker compute shrinks as $T_{\text{compute}}/N$, while communication and synchronization overheads ($T_{\text{comm}} + T_{\text{sync}}$) remain flat or grow with $N$. As $N \to \infty$, the communication-to-compute ratio $\rho$ explodes, driving scaling efficiency $\eta_{\text{scaling}} \to 0$. Choice A confuses falling per-worker compute with rising system efficiency. Choice C is incorrect because even bandwidth-optimal collectives cannot eliminate latency and scaling walls. Choice D is false because Adam communicates identical gradient tensor volumes as SGD.
questions.learning_objective: Interpret how the communication-to-compute ratio limits scaling efficiency as worker count grows

questions.question: Explain the difference between hardware efficiency and statistical efficiency in a distributed training run, and give a concrete scenario where a cluster configuration wins on one and loses on the other.
questions.answer: Hardware efficiency measures how effectively the cluster's physical compute capacity (TFLOP/s) translates into step throughput (samples/sec), penalized by communication, synchronization barriers, and kernel launch overheads. Statistical efficiency measures how effectively processed samples reduce the training loss (loss reduction per sample). In a scenario where batch size is scaled far beyond the critical batch size $B_{\text{crit}}$ across 1,024 GPUs, hardware efficiency may remain high (high MFU and fast step times), but statistical efficiency collapses because gradient updates become redundant; as a result, total training time and cost to reach target validation loss increase despite high hardware throughput.
questions.learning_objective: Compare time-per-step hardware efficiency with convergence-per-sample statistical efficiency in distributed optimization

questions.question: Why does Stale-Synchronous Parallel (SSP) training typically require a smaller effective learning rate than Bulk-Synchronous Parallel (BSP) at the same global batch size?
choices: Because bounded parameter staleness introduces an additional variance/gradient error term that destabilizes updates unless damped by a smaller learning rate
Because SSP workers compute exact full-batch gradients instead of stochastic minibatches
Because SSP eliminates all network communication between workers
Because SSP only functions with second-order quasi-Newton optimizers
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Bounded staleness introduces gradient error requiring learning rate damping. In SSP, workers compute gradients against parameter snapshots that may be up to $\tau_{\text{stale}}$ steps behind the most recent model state. This staleness introduces an error term proportional to $\tau_{\text{stale}} \cdot \eta \cdot \|\nabla \mathcal{L}\|$ into the optimization trajectory; reducing the learning rate $\eta$ is necessary to bound this staleness penalty and prevent divergence. Choice B is false because SSP uses stochastic minibatches. Choice C is incorrect because SSP still synchronizes parameters asynchronously over the network. Choice D is false because SSP is routinely used with standard first-order optimizers like SGD and Adam.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how bounded staleness changes optimizer tuning in distributed training

questions.question: A team scales a run's global batch size from 512 to 4,096 by moving from 8 to 64 data-parallel workers. The model is operating comfortably below its critical batch size. Which learning-rate adjustment is the default rule, and what complement must accompany it?
choices: Keep the learning rate unchanged, because large-batch variance reduction automatically stabilizes training without adjustment
Multiply the learning rate by 64, matching the total worker count rather than the batch-size ratio
Multiply the learning rate by $\sqrt{8}$ from step zero without warmup, because linear scaling only applies to inference
Multiply the learning rate by 8 and include a warmup schedule to allow optimizer statistics to stabilize
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Multiply learning rate by $8\times$ with linear learning rate warmup. Below the critical batch size, the linear scaling rule ($\eta_{\text{new}} = \eta_{\text{base}} \times (B_{\text{new}} / B_{\text{base}}) = 8\eta_{\text{base}}$) preserves optimization dynamics by scaling the parameter step proportionally to the $8\times$ reduction in gradient variance. Learning rate warmup (gradually ramping $\eta$ from 0 over initial epochs) is essential to prevent early optimization instability while Adam moment buffers or initial weights calibrate. Choice A results in under-utilizing the large batch, requiring unnecessarily many steps. Choice B scales by worker count ($64\times$) rather than batch scaling factor ($8\times$). Choice C incorrectly applies square-root scaling (a heuristic for regimes near/past critical batch size) without necessary warmup.
questions.learning_objective: Apply linear learning-rate scaling with warmup for a concrete 8x batch-size increase below the critical batch size

questions.question: What happens to optimization progress and training throughput when the global batch size is scaled significantly beyond a model's critical batch size ($B \gg B_{\text{crit}}$)?
choices: Step throughput increases linearly and total training steps to reach target loss decrease proportionally, yielding ideal speedup
The model immediately diverges regardless of learning rate adjustments or warmup schedules
Step throughput may increase, but returns in loss reduction per sample diminish sharply, causing total computational work (total FLOPs to target loss) to increase
Hardware Model Flops Utilization (MFU) drops to zero because gradient variance vanishes completely
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Diminishing statistical returns and increased total compute to target loss. Past the critical batch size $B_{\text{crit}}$, gradient estimates become saturated with redundant information; doubling the batch size yields diminishing reductions in required optimization steps. While hardware step throughput (samples/sec) may scale with added workers, the total number of processed tokens/FLOPs required to achieve target loss increases, eroding cost efficiency. Choice A is false because linear scaling breaks down past $B_{\text{crit}}$. Choice B is incorrect because training can remain stable if learning rates are properly damped (e.g. square-root scaling). Choice D is false because hardware MFU depends on kernel efficiency, not gradient variance.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the diminishing statistical returns and compute inflation that occur past the critical batch size

questions.question: A 64-worker BSP run reaches target loss in 20 percent fewer total samples than a 64-worker SSP run on the same cluster, but the SSP run has 30 percent lower per-step communication overhead. How should an engineer reason about this trade-off when the cluster has a few known straggler nodes?
questions.answer: The decision depends on total wall-clock time to target loss: $\text{Time} = \text{Steps to Convergence} \times \text{Step Time}$. In BSP, a single straggler delays all 64 workers at every synchronization barrier, inflating average step time and tail latency (p99). In SSP, workers compute through bounded staleness ($\tau$), eliminating barrier stalls behind stragglers and reducing step time by 30%. If the cluster has frequent stragglers such that barrier waiting in BSP accounts for >20% of step time, SSP's lower step latency outweighs its 20% sample efficiency penalty, resulting in faster wall-clock convergence. If the cluster is highly homogeneous with minimal straggler tail latency, BSP's superior sample efficiency wins.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate a BSP-vs-SSP trade-off using both statistical efficiency and measured straggler behavior

sparse parameter servers / embedding sharding vs dense collectives

questions.question: A team runs ZeRO-3 on a large transformer and finds per-GPU memory is still exhausted during the forward pass, even though parameters, gradients, and optimizer states are sharded across 256 workers. What is the primary source of memory pressure causing this OOM?
choices: ZeRO-3 increases optimizer memory so much that gradients no longer fit on any device
ZeRO-3 prevents backward propagation from executing across multiple nodes
Activation memory — the intermediate activations generated during the forward pass scaling with $B \times S \times d_{\text{model}}$ — is not sharded across data-parallel workers
Data parallelism prohibits the use of activation checkpointing (recomputation)
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Unsharded activation memory scaling with sequence length and batch size. ZeRO-3 shards static model states (weights, gradients, optimizer moments) across data-parallel ranks, but each rank must still hold the dynamic activations generated by its local batch shard ($B_{\text{local}} \times S \times d_{\text{model}} \times N_{\text{layers}}$). For long sequence lengths $S$ or deep models, activation memory exceeds GPU HBM capacity, necessitating model parallelism (tensor or pipeline parallelism) or sequence parallelism to shard activation tensors. Choice A is false because ZeRO-3 drastically reduces optimizer memory. Choice B and D are false because backward passes and activation checkpointing work seamlessly with ZeRO-3.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why activation memory can force model parallelism even when ZeRO-3 has already sharded all static state

questions.question: Pipeline parallelism routinely runs across nodes on InfiniBand, but tensor parallelism is almost always confined within a single NVLink-connected node. Explain the communication-structure reason for this split, naming the messages each strategy actually sends.
questions.answer: Pipeline parallelism partitions layers sequentially across stages and communicates only boundary activation tensors ($B \times S \times d_{\text{model}}$) point-to-point (P2P) between adjacent stages once per microbatch; this low-frequency, point-to-point traffic easily fits within InfiniBand bandwidth (50–100 GB/s). In contrast, Megatron-style tensor parallelism splits intra-layer GEMM matrices and executes two AllReduce collectives per transformer layer (one for attention, one for MLP) on every forward and backward pass. For deep models with dozens of layers, TP generates high-frequency, latency-sensitive AllReduce operations that require the massive bandwidth (>900 GB/s) and sub-microsecond latency of NVLink to prevent compute stalls.
questions.learning_objective: Compare the communication volume, frequency, and bandwidth requirements of pipeline and tensor parallelism

questions.question: Megatron-style tensor parallelism reduces inter-GPU communication to exactly two AllReduce operations per transformer block. What architectural design choice makes that possible?
choices: Using only row-parallel linear layers throughout the entire transformer block
Replacing multi-head attention with parameter servers to avoid collective communication
Executing tensor parallelism exclusively during the backward pass while running the forward pass redundantly
Pairing a column-parallel linear layer followed by a row-parallel linear layer so intermediate activations remain partitioned and require no synchronization
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Column-parallel followed by row-parallel linear layer factoring. In Megatron-LM, the first linear layer in both multi-head attention (QKV projection) and MLP (first feed-forward) is column-partitioned (splitting output dimension), producing column-sharded activations. The second linear layer (attention output projection and second MLP layer) is row-partitioned (splitting input dimension), directly consuming the column-sharded activations without any intermediate network communication. A single AllReduce is needed only at the end of each sub-block (after the row-parallel projection) to sum partial results before the residual connection. Choice A would require an AllGather between layers. Choice B is irrelevant to dense LLM tensor parallelism. Choice C is incorrect because forward GEMMs must also be partitioned.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the column-then-row transformer-block factoring as the design choice that minimizes tensor-parallel AllReduce frequency

questions.question: A production recommendation system has a 10 TB embedding table with sparse lookups — each minibatch touches roughly 0.01 percent of the embedding rows. Which distributed architecture best matches this workload, and why?
choices: Parameter servers or sharded embedding tables with sparse pull/push operations, transferring only the accessed row vectors
Dense Ring AllReduce across all workers, because all devices must synchronize the entire 10 TB table every step
Tensor parallelism within an 8-GPU node, because embedding tables have identical communication patterns to dense MLP layers
Pipeline parallelism across 100 stages, because embeddings naturally form the first stage of the network
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Parameter servers or sharded embedding tables with sparse pull/push operations. When lookups are sparse (touching only 0.01% of a 10 TB table, or ~1 GB per step), parameter servers or dedicated embedding sharding (table-wise/row-wise) allow workers to exchange only the sparse gradient vectors for accessed indices via point-to-point pull/push operations. Choice B is a massive anti-pattern that would attempt to AllReduce 10 TB of dense data per step, saturating any network. Choice C fails because embedding lookups are index gathers, not dense GEMMs. Choice D does not solve the memory capacity or sparse communication problem.
questions.learning_objective: Select a distributed architecture whose communication pattern matches the sparsity of the workload's parameter accesses

questions.question: Why does increasing the number of pipeline stages ($p$) in pipeline parallelism not automatically yield a linear increase in training throughput?
choices: Because pipeline parallelism requires an AllReduce collective across all stages on every microbatch forward pass

Because deeper pipelines increase the pipeline bubble fraction $F_{\text{bubble}} = \frac{p-1}{m + p - 1}$, causing GPUs to sit idle during startup and teardown phases unless microbatch count ($m$) increases
Because activations cannot be stored across stage boundaries without converting them to INT4 precision
Because deeper pipelines force all workers to use asynchronous parameter server updates
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Pipeline bubble overhead ($F_{\text{bubble}}$) scales with stage count. In pipeline parallelism, GPUs experience idle time (the bubble) while waiting for activations to propagate forward and gradients to flow backward during pipeline ramp-up and drain. The bubble fraction is $F_{\text{bubble}} = (p-1)/(m + p - 1)$, where $p$ is the number of stages and $m$ is the number of microbatches. Increasing $p$ without scaling $m$ inflates bubble idle time, offsetting the compute benefits of adding stages. Choice A is false because PP uses point-to-point peer-to-peer transfers, not AllReduce. Choice C is false because activations are passed in native precision (BF16/FP16). Choice D is unrelated to pipeline execution.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze the pipeline bubble overhead formula and explain how stage count and microbatch count affect utilization

questions.question: Explain how Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models allow parameter capacity to scale while keeping per-token compute FLOPs roughly constant, and identify the primary distributed networking bottleneck introduced by this architecture.
questions.answer: MoE replaces dense Feed-Forward Network (FFN) layers with $E$ separate expert networks and a routing gate. For each token, the router selects only top-$k$ experts (e.g., $k=2$ out of $E=64$), so total parameter memory scales linearly with $E$ while per-token FLOPs remain fixed to $k$ experts. However, because tokens in a batch are routed dynamically to different expert devices across the cluster, MoE introduces an All-to-All collective communication pattern (dispatch and combine) at every MoE layer. This All-to-All collective creates dense, all-pairs traffic that heavily stresses cross-rack bisection bandwidth, making MoE throughput highly susceptible to network congestion and expert load imbalance.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how sparse expert activation trades dense compute for bisection-bandwidth-intensive token routing

dynamic delayed scaling to prevent underflow/overflow across shifting magnitudes

rationale.question_strategy: Match E4M3/E5M2 formats to forward weights vs backward gradients in an MCQ, explain dynamic delayed scaling in a SHORT question, and clarify FP8 training execution roles with FP32 master weights in an MCQ.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Format allocation -> numerical scaling mechanism -> runtime training architecture.
rationale.integration: Connects low-precision hardware acceleration (Tensor Cores) to distributed memory reduction and numerical optimization stability.
rationale.ranking_explanation: FP8 is standard for modern LLM distributed training on Hopper and Blackwell architectures.

questions.question: In the three-precision FP8 training recipe, what are the distinct roles assigned to the E4M3 and E5M2 formats?
choices: E4M3 is used exclusively for gradients; E5M2 is used exclusively for weights and activations
E4M3 is used for optimizer momentum buffers; E5M2 is used for post-training INT8 quantization
E4M3 and E5M2 are interchangeable and used randomly to balance floating-point rounding errors
E4M3 (4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits) is used for forward activations and weights; E5M2 (5 exponent bits, 2 mantissa bits) is used for backward gradients
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. E4M3 for weights/activations, E5M2 for gradients. E4M3 allocates 3 bits to the mantissa, providing higher numerical precision (fewer rounding errors) at the cost of narrower dynamic range ($[-448, 448]$), making it well-suited for forward activations and weights. E5M2 allocates 5 bits to the exponent, matching FP16's dynamic range ($[-57344, 57344]$) at the expense of mantissa precision, which is necessary to capture the wide dynamic range of backpropagated gradients across deep networks. Choice A inverts the assignments. Choice B is incorrect because optimizer states are maintained in FP32/BF16. Choice C is false because the two formats have fundamentally different numerical characteristics.
questions.learning_objective: Match each FP8 format to the training quantity whose range-precision profile it supports

questions.question: Why is dynamic delayed scaling necessary in FP8 distributed training, and what failure occurs if a single static scale factor is used across the entire training run?
questions.answer: FP8 has a vastly restricted representable dynamic range compared to FP16/BF16 (e.g., $[-448, 448]$ for E4M3). During training, tensor magnitudes shift across iterations and layers. If a fixed static scale factor is used, small gradient/activation tensors will underflow to zero (causing gradient vanishing and frozen weights), while large tensors will overflow to maximum representable values or NaNs (causing catastrophic instability). Dynamic delayed scaling tracks maximum absolute values ($a_{\text{max}}$) across recent iterations and dynamically adjusts per-tensor scale factors ($S = \text{FP8}_{\text{max}} / a_{\text{max}}$) to keep values mapped into the optimal representable range without requiring synchronous reductions on every step.
questions.learning_objective: Explain how dynamic scaling preserves numerical stability and prevents underflow/overflow across shifting tensor magnitudes in FP8 training

questions.question: In modern distributed training on Hopper- and Blackwell-class GPUs, what is the operational role of FP8 within the training execution stack?
choices: FP8 is used exclusively as a post-training compression format for inference deployment
FP8 is used for compute-intensive GEMM operations in forward and backward passes, while master weights and optimizer updates remain in FP32
FP8 replaces all tensors including optimizer states, master weights, and loss calculation buffers with zero FP32 state
FP8 is used solely for inter-node network transmission, with all compute executed in FP64
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. FP8 for GEMM operations with FP32 master weights and optimizer states. In modern FP8 mixed-precision training (such as NVIDIA Transformer Engine), matrix multiplications in both forward and backward passes execute in FP8 (E4M3/E5M2) to achieve 2x Tensor Core throughput and reduce activation memory, while master weights, weight updates, and Adam optimizer states are preserved in FP32 to ensure numerical stability and convergence. Choice A describes post-training quantization, not training. Choice C is incorrect because full FP8 optimizer states cause divergence. Choice D is false because compute is accelerated directly in FP8 on Tensor Cores.
questions.learning_objective: Distinguish FP8 training-time compute acceleration from post-training inference quantization

questions.question: A frontier LLM training configuration runs TP=8, PP=16, and DP=128 ($N=16,384$ GPUs). If the team doubles the cluster size to 32,768 GPUs by scaling DP to 256 while keeping TP=8 and PP=16 constant, which communication domain's traffic increases?
choices: Intra-node TP AllReduce traffic increases by 2x
Inter-node PP point-to-point activation volume increases by 2x
Data-parallel gradient reduction group size and aggregate cross-pod AllReduce traffic increase, while TP and PP communication remain unchanged
All three parallelism dimensions experience doubled communication volume per step
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. DP gradient AllReduce traffic scales while TP and PP remain constant. In 3D parallelism, the communication domains are orthogonal. TP communication occurs strictly within each 8-GPU tensor-parallel group (intra-node), and PP communication occurs strictly between adjacent stages in the 16-stage pipeline. Doubling the DP degree from 128 to 256 expands only the data-parallel communicators across nodes/pods; the intra-node TP AllReduce and PP P2P transfers per worker remain completely unchanged. Choices A, B, and D fail to recognize the domain isolation of 3D parallelism.
questions.learning_objective: Identify which communication domain's traffic grows when one axis of a 3D parallelism configuration is scaled

questions.question: When mapping a 3D parallelism configuration (TP, PP, DP) onto a physical cluster hierarchy consisting of NVLink intra-node, InfiniBand inter-node within a rack, and inter-rack/inter-pod network links, what is the standard placement strategy?
choices: TP within nodes (NVLink), PP across nodes within a spine/fabric domain (InfiniBand), and DP across nodes/pods
DP within nodes (NVLink), TP across racks (Ethernet), and PP across pods
PP within nodes (NVLink), DP across nodes (InfiniBand), and TP across pods (Ethernet)
TP, PP, and DP distributed randomly across nodes via round-robin assignment
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. TP inside nodes (NVLink), PP across nodes (InfiniBand), DP across pods. Tensor parallelism requires high-frequency, sub-millisecond AllReduce operations on every layer, demanding intra-node NVLink (>900 GB/s). Pipeline parallelism transmits only stage-boundary activations point-to-point, making it well-suited for inter-node InfiniBand fabrics. Data parallelism synchronizes once per step (or microbatch accumulation window) and can overlap with backward compute, making it the most tolerant of cross-pod/cross-rack network latencies. Choices B, C, and D violate the physical bandwidth hierarchy by placing latency-critical TP traffic across slow network links.
questions.learning_objective: Map TP, PP, and DP onto a cluster hierarchy based on their per-step communication frequency and volume

questions.question: Explain why training a 1-trillion parameter dense model cannot be accomplished using pure data parallelism, pure tensor parallelism, or pure pipeline parallelism alone on currently available hardware.
questions.answer:
A 1T-parameter model in mixed precision requires ~16 TB for training state (weights, gradients, 16-bit Adam, FP32 master weights) plus terabytes of activation memory:
1. Pure DP fails because a single GPU (80–192 GB HBM) cannot hold even a fraction of the 16 TB model state.
2. Pure TP fails because TP requires per-layer AllReduce; scaling TP beyond a single NVLink node (e.g. to $t=128$) across InfiniBand/Ethernet causes massive communication latency that stalls compute.
3. Pure PP fails because scaling PP to $p=128$ stages creates an unmanageable pipeline bubble ($F_{\text{bubble}} \approx (p-1)/(m+p-1)$), requiring thousands of microbatches that explode peak activation memory.
Frontier models require 3D hybrid parallelism: TP=8 fits intra-node NVLink, PP=8–16 partitions layers across nodes with manageable bubbles, and DP scales out throughput across the remaining cluster.
questions.learning_objective: Justify why frontier-scale training requires composing multiple parallelism dimensions rather than selecting one

questions.question: In a hybrid 3D training step (TP=8, PP=8, DP=64), which synchronization operation represents the largest total data volume communicated across the cluster network per global step?
choices: Data-parallel gradient AllReduce across the 64 DP replicas
Point-to-point activation passing between adjacent pipeline stages
Forward-pass AllReduce within each 8-GPU tensor-parallel group
Master weight broadcasting from rank 0 to all workers
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Data-parallel gradient AllReduce across DP replicas. While TP AllReduce has the highest frequency (executed twice per layer per microbatch within NVLink), the total volume of data synchronized across the global cluster network is dominated by the DP gradient AllReduce, which exchanges gradients for the entire model across all 64 DP replicas at the end of the step. PP transfers only boundary activation tensors ($B \times S \times d_{\text{model}}$), which is orders of magnitude smaller. Choice D is incorrect because DP uses symmetric AllReduce rather than centralized master weight broadcasts.
questions.learning_objective: Identify the cluster-wide synchronization event whose aggregate volume dominates one global 3D training step

questions.question: In a 3D parallelism setup, what is the primary systems trade-off when reducing pipeline parallelism depth (e.g. from PP=16 to PP=8) while keeping total GPU count constant by doubling data parallelism (DP)?
choices: Throughput decreases because pipeline bubbles expand when PP depth is reduced
Memory consumption per GPU decreases because fewer stages are active simultaneously
The pipeline bubble fraction ($F_{\text{bubble}}$) shrinks and throughput improves, but per-GPU model parameter and activation memory footprint increases
Communication volume across the cluster drops to zero because pipeline stages no longer communicate
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Smaller pipeline bubble and higher utilization at the cost of higher per-GPU memory. Halving PP depth from 16 to 8 doubles the number of layers assigned to each stage, which halves the pipeline bubble fraction $F_{\text{bubble}} = (p-1)/(m+p-1)$ and improves hardware utilization. However, each GPU must now store twice as many layer weights, optimizer states, and forward activations, increasing per-device memory pressure. Choice A is false because bubble size decreases with smaller $p$. Choice B is false because each GPU holds more layers. Choice D is false because adjacent PP stages still exchange activations and DP AllReduce volume increases.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate the utilization-vs-memory trade-off when changing pipeline depth

questions.question: Blackwell-era accelerators offer roughly double the previous NVLink bandwidth per GPU (up to 1.8 TB/s) and larger NVLink switch domains (e.g. NVL72 connecting 72 GPUs over a single NVLink fabric). Explain how this architectural shift alters optimal 3D hybrid parallelism configurations for frontier models.
questions.answer: In Hopper/A100 clusters, the NVLink domain is confined to 8 GPUs per server, forcing tensor parallelism to $\text{TP} \le 8$ and requiring pipeline parallelism ($\text{PP}=8\text{--}16$) across InfiniBand to fit models exceeding 8 GPUs. With NVL72 providing a unified 1.8 TB/s NVLink domain across 72 GPUs, the feasible tensor-parallel degree expands to $\text{TP}=16\text{--}64$ without paying inter-node InfiniBand latency penalties. This allows system architects to drastically reduce or eliminate pipeline parallelism ($\text{PP}=1$ or $2$), virtually eliminating pipeline bubble overheads ($F_{\text{bubble}} \to 0$) and simplifying microbatch scheduling, while dedicating the remaining cluster scaling to data parallelism.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how next-generation interconnect changes shift the optimal 3D parallelism mix and relocate the binding system constraint

alternating execution regimes: memory-bound rollout generation vs compute-bound training
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) architectural simplification

sequence length variance and load imbalance at synchronization barriers
rationale.question_strategy: Identify active training vs inference models in an MCQ, analyze infrastructure asymmetry in a SHORT reflection, evaluate DPO resource reduction in an MCQ, probe rollout MFU limits in an MCQ, and diagnose sequence-length variance stragglers in an MCQ.
rationale.difficulty_progression: Memory budgeting -> orchestration asymmetry -> algorithmic simplification (DPO) -> hardware arithmetic intensity -> batching/synchronization stragglers.
rationale.integration: Connects distributed training to post-training alignment pipelines, inference serving dynamics (KV caches), and heterogeneous cluster orchestration.

questions.question: In standard 4-model PPO-style RLHF (Policy, Reference, Reward, Value models), which models require active optimizer state, gradient buffers, and backward passes during the training phase?
choices: Reference model and Reward model
Policy model and Value (critic) model
All four models (Policy, Reference, Reward, Value)
Only the Reward model
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Policy model and Value (critic) model. In PPO alignment, only the Policy (actor) and Value (critic) networks are updated via gradient descent, requiring parameters, gradients, and optimizer states (e.g., Adam FP32 moments). The Reference model (which provides KL penalty regularization) and the Reward model (which scores generated responses) are frozen; they participate strictly in forward-pass inference and require zero gradient or optimizer memory. Choice A names the frozen inference models. Choice C is a major memory-budgeting pitfall that overestimates training memory by 2x. Choice D is incorrect because the reward model is frozen during RLHF.
questions.learning_objective: Identify which RLHF components require full training-state memory versus inference-only memory

questions.question: Explain why PPO-based RLHF creates a severe infrastructure orchestration and resource utilization bottleneck compared to standard pretraining.
questions.answer:
PPO RLHF combines two fundamentally asymmetric workloads in an alternating step loop:
1. Rollout Phase: The policy model generates autoregressive responses token-by-token (inference), which is memory-bandwidth bound (low arithmetic intensity, low MFU, high KV cache memory).
2. Training Phase: The policy and value models perform forward/backward passes on generated trajectories using SGD/Adam (training), which is compute-bound (dense matrix multiplies, high MFU).
Because the rollout generation and training phases alternate synchronously within every PPO iteration, GPUs dedicated to training sit idle during generation, or GPUs dedicated to generation sit idle during training, causing overall cluster Model Flops Utilization (MFU) to drop significantly below pretraining levels.
questions.learning_objective: Explain why RLHF alternates between inference-like and training-like cluster regimes within each step

questions.question: Why does Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) drastically simplify distributed cluster orchestration and reduce memory footprint compared to PPO?
choices: DPO eliminates the Reference model and trains the Policy using reinforcement learning on a central parameter server
DPO runs exclusively in INT4 on single-GPU edge devices without requiring distributed training
DPO replaces gradient descent with evolutionary search, eliminating backpropagation entirely
DPO analytically substitutes the reward and value functions directly into the policy loss, eliminating the Reward model, Value model, and online autoregressive rollout generation phase
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Analytical elimination of Reward model, Value model, and online rollout generation. DPO reparameterizes the RLHF objective to derive an exact closed-form solution for the optimal policy under the Bradley-Terry preference model. This allows direct supervised training on static preference pairs using only the Policy and frozen Reference models. It eliminates the separate Reward model, Value (critic) network, and the costly online autoregressive response generation phase, transforming RLHF into standard compute-bound training. Choice A is false because DPO retains the reference model. Choices B and C misrepresent the mathematics and execution of DPO.
questions.learning_objective: Compare PPO and DPO resource demands and identify which components and phases DPO eliminates

questions.question: Why is Model Flops Utilization (MFU) during the rollout generation phase of PPO RLHF typically much lower (15–30%) than MFU during pretraining (45–60%)?
choices: Because the policy model parameters are converted to FP64 precision during generation
Because autoregressive generation produces tokens sequentially with small batch sizes, making execution memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute-bound
Because NCCL AllReduce collectives are executed after every single token generation step across all GPUs
Because reinforcement learning loss functions cannot utilize GPU Tensor Cores
questions.answer: The correct answer is B. Memory-bandwidth bound autoregressive token generation. Pretraining processes large batches of packed tokens in parallel using large matrix-matrix multiplications (GEMMs) with high arithmetic intensity ($O(\text{FLOPs}) \gg O(\text{Bytes})$), fully saturating Tensor Cores. Autoregressive rollout generation in RLHF generates tokens sequentially: for each new token, all model weights and KV caches must be fetched from HBM to compute a small matrix-vector product (GEMV), making the workload memory-bandwidth bound and capping MFU far below peak Tensor Core capacity. Choice A is false because generation runs in BF16/FP16/FP8. Choice C is false because generation within a replica requires no cross-replica AllReduce per token. Choice D is incorrect because Tensor Cores can be used for any linear operation.
questions.learning_objective: Recognize why autoregressive rollout is bandwidth-bound and why its MFU trails training MFU

questions.question: RLHF preference datasets exhibit large variance in response lengths (e.g. 50 to 2,048 tokens). In a distributed training setup, what happens if variable-length responses are padded to the maximum sequence length across minibatches?
choices: Compute efficiency collapses due to wasted FLOPs on pad tokens, and workers processing shorter responses sit idle waiting at synchronization barriers for workers processing long sequences
Communication speed increases because padded tokens compress automatically over InfiniBand
Memory consumption decreases because padding replaces dynamic memory allocations with static zeros
Gradient updates become mathematically exact because all batches have identical dimensional shapes
questions.answer: The correct answer is A. Wasted compute on padding and synchronization stragglers. Padding all sequences to the maximum length causes quadratic ($S^2$) or linear ($S$) compute waste on non-informative pad tokens. In distributed training, workers assigned batches containing mostly short sequences finish their forward/backward passes much faster than workers assigned long sequences, creating severe load imbalance and straggler delays at the AllReduce gradient barrier. Systems address this through sequence packing and variable-length attention kernels (e.g. FlashAttention varlen). Choice B is false because zero-padding is transmitted across the network unless sparse packing is used. Choice C is false because padding increases peak memory. Choice D is false because pad tokens must be masked out to prevent corrupted gradients.
questions.learning_objective: Analyze how sequence-length variance degrades both compute efficiency and synchronization balance in distributed RLHF

questions.question: A 120B-parameter model exceeds the memory of any single 8-GPU NVLink node, the dataset contains 2 trillion tokens, and training must complete within 30 days on a 2,048-GPU cluster connected via InfiniBand. Applying the chapter's decision framework, which parallelism configuration is most suitable?
choices: Pure Data Parallelism with standard DDP across all 2,048 GPUs
Pure Pipeline Parallelism with PP=2,048 stages across all GPUs
Pure Tensor Parallelism with TP=2,048 across the entire InfiniBand fabric
Hybrid 3D Parallelism combining intra-node TP=8, inter-node PP=4, and DP=64 across the cluster
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. Hybrid 3D Parallelism (TP=8, PP=4, DP=64). The 120B model (~240 GB parameters, ~960 GB training state) exceeds a single GPU (80 GB) and a single 8-GPU node (640 GB). Therefore, intra-node TP=8 shards the layers across NVLink, while inter-node PP=4 splits the 120B model across 4 nodes (32 GPUs per pipeline replica) over InfiniBand with minimal bubble overhead. The remaining cluster capacity is allocated to DP=64 ($32 \times 64 = 2048$ GPUs) to achieve the throughput needed for 2 trillion tokens in 30 days. Choice A is impossible because the model does not fit in single-GPU memory. Choice B suffers from a catastrophic pipeline bubble ($F_{\text{bubble}} \to 1$). Choice C stalls due to cross-node per-layer AllReduce over InfiniBand.
questions.learning_objective: Apply the chapter's decision framework to select hybrid parallelism over tempting pure-strategy or FSDP-only alternatives under combined memory and topology constraints

questions.question: Explain why implementation complexity is substantially higher for hybrid parallelism than for plain data parallelism, and name two concrete engineering responsibilities that hybrid adds.
questions.answer:
Plain data parallelism wraps an existing single-device training graph with an AllReduce hook (e.g., `DistributedDataParallel`), requiring no changes to model definitions or execution graphs. In contrast, hybrid parallelism requires:
1. Manual Model Partitioning: Rewriting layer implementations into column-parallel and row-parallel linear projections (for TP) and explicitly slicing the network into balanced sequential sub-graphs across physical pipeline stages (for PP).
2. Complex Scheduling and Group Management: Orchestrating microbatch schedules (e.g. 1F1B or interleaved 1F1B) to minimize pipeline bubbles and activation memory, while managing distinct multidimensional NCCL process groups (TP, PP, and DP communicators) across heterogeneous interconnect tiers.
questions.learning_objective: Justify why integrating multiple parallelism dimensions raises implementation complexity and identify the specific engineering responsibilities that compose

questions.question: Why is there no single distributed training strategy (among DP, FSDP, TP, PP, and Hybrid) that strictly dominates all others across all training workloads?
choices: Because distributed training algorithms are non-deterministic and performance fluctuates randomly between runs
Because different deep learning frameworks (PyTorch, JAX, TensorFlow) forbid the use of competing parallelism methods
Because each strategy navigates orthogonal engineering trade-offs across memory capacity, communication frequency, interconnect bandwidth limits, and implementation complexity
Because hardware vendors restrict tensor parallelism to proprietary hardware while data parallelism runs on all chips
questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Orthogonal trade-offs across memory, communication frequency, fabric hierarchy, and complexity. No single strategy dominates because training is a multi-constraint satisfaction problem: Data Parallelism is simple and compute-efficient but requires full model replication; FSDP saves memory but incurs extra collective latency on the critical path; Tensor Parallelism reduces per-layer memory but requires ultra-high NVLink bandwidth (>900 GB/s); Pipeline Parallelism crosses slow networks but introduces idle pipeline bubbles. The optimal choice is dictated by parameter count, activation memory, cluster network topology, and batch size constraints. Choice A is false because distributed algorithms follow deterministic physical cost models. Choice B and D are false because modern open-source frameworks support all parallelism strategies across standard accelerator hardware.
questions.learning_objective: Evaluate distributed parallelism choices as a multidimensional trade-off rather than a universal ranking

questions.question: A framework exposes a one-line wrapper (such as PyTorch DistributedDataParallel) that makes data parallelism appear trivial to the user. Which critical runtime optimizations is the framework executing under the hood?
choices: Recompiling model weights into FP8 format and replacing SGD with evolutionary optimization
Converting dense matrix multiplications into sparse lookups on a remote parameter server

Gradient bucketing to coalesce small parameter tensors into bandwidth-saturating messages, overlapping backward computation with AllReduce communication, and autotuning collective algorithms for cluster topology

questions.answer: The correct answer is C. Gradient bucketing, compute-communication overlap, and topology-aware collective execution. A production DDP wrapper hides substantial runtime machinery: (1) Gradient Bucketing: coalescing hundreds of small layer gradient tensors into large contiguous memory buckets (e.g. 25 MB) to saturate network bandwidth; (2) Overlap: registering autograd backward hooks to launch non-blocking AllReduce on completed buckets while earlier layers continue backpropagation; (3) NCCL Integration: detecting physical topology (NVLink vs. PCIe vs. InfiniBand) to select optimal ring or tree communication trees. Choice A describes quantization and unrelated optimizers. Choice B describes parameter servers. Choice D describes asynchronous training (ASP), which breaks standard DDP mathematical equivalence.

questions.question: Explain why tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism require more intrusive and explicit framework abstractions than standard data parallelism.
questions.answer:
Standard data parallelism treats the neural network as an opaque black box: it executes the unaltered single-device computation graph and intercepts only the resulting gradients at the end of the backward pass via autograd hooks. In contrast, tensor and pipeline parallelism structurally alter the execution graph:
- Tensor Parallelism requires surgically rewriting model layers (e.g. splitting linear weight matrices into column-parallel and row-parallel slices and embedding custom AllReduce/AllGather primitives directly inside the forward/backward graph).
- Pipeline Parallelism requires partitioning the layer graph into discrete sequential sub-graphs, inserting cross-device point-to-point communication buffers, and managing complex microbatch schedules (1F1B) across independent device runtimes.
questions.learning_objective: Compare the abstraction demands of data-parallel wrappers with the explicit structural knowledge required by model- and pipeline-parallel frameworks

questions.question: Consider one full forward-and-backward pass of a single transformer layer under Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP / ZeRO-3). In what exact order must the runtime execute collective communication primitives to compute the layer?
choices: 1. ReduceScatter parameter shards -> 2. Forward GEMM -> 3. AllGather gradient shards -> 4. Backward GEMM
1. AllReduce parameters -> 2. Forward GEMM -> 3. AllReduce gradients -> 4. Backward GEMM
1. Broadcast parameters from rank 0 -> 2. Forward GEMM -> 3. Scatter gradients to rank 0 -> 4. Backward GEMM

1. AllGather parameter shards before forward -> 2. Forward GEMM -> 3. Discard unpartitioned weights -> 4. AllGather parameter shards before backward -> 5. Backward GEMM -> 6. ReduceScatter gradient shards
questions.answer: The correct answer is D. AllGather parameters before forward -> Discard -> AllGather parameters before backward -> ReduceScatter gradients. In FSDP, each GPU holds only $1/N$ of the layer's weights. Before the forward pass, an AllGather reconstructs the full layer weights; once the forward GEMM finishes, unpartitioned weights are freed from memory. In the backward pass, an AllGather reconstructs the weights again to compute input activations and parameter gradients; finally, a ReduceScatter simultaneously sums gradients across workers and scatters the reduced $1/N$ gradient shard to its owner rank. Choice A inverts the required collective order. Choice B uses AllReduce, failing to shard state. Choice C uses centralized broadcast/scatter, creating rank-0 bottlenecks.
